The authors propose several methods for determining when to route a query to the stronger model, primarily based on the consistency of the weaker model's answers. These methods include a vote-based approach, where a threshold on the consistency score is used, and a verification-based approach, which checks if the most consistent answers from different prompts match. Furthermore, the authors introduce a mixture of thought representations, sampling answers from both chain-of-thought and program-of-thought prompts to enhance the performance of the weaker model. The empirical evaluation, conducted on six reasoning benchmark datasets, demonstrates that the proposed approach achieves comparable performance to using the stronger model alone, while significantly reducing costs, requiring only 40% of the stronger model's resources. The paper's main contribution lies in its practical approach to cost-effective LLM utilization, offering a valuable strategy for deploying these powerful models in resource-constrained environments. The authors also explore the impact of different prompting strategies and demonstrate the effectiveness of their proposed mixture of thought representations. The findings suggest that by carefully managing the use of weaker and stronger models, it is possible to achieve a balance between accuracy and cost-efficiency in LLM-based reasoning tasks. The paper's exploration of different consistency measures, including sampling with different chain-of-thought and program-of-thought prompts, is also a valuable contribution.
